e.etymology: A respelling of Colter, an English surname usually explained as a name for someone who looked after colts. Mountain man John Colter made the surname part of the lore of the American West.
A spelling variant of Lauren, a feminine form of Laurence, from Latin Laurentius (man from Laurentum), long tied to the laurel. Singer Lauryn Hill made this spelling familiar in the late 1990s.
namesakes: Lauryn Hill (singer and rapper, The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill)

assoc.t: Lauryn Hill, singer and rapper of the Fugees

e.etymology: From the French surname of fashion designer Coco Chanel, whose couture house and No. 5 perfume made it a byword for luxury. The surname goes back to an Old French word for a channel or pipe.
namesakes: Chanel Iman (model)
Chanel West Coast (rapper and Ridiculousness host)

assoc.t: French luxury fashion and perfume house

e.etymology: The Scandinavian form of Henry, from Old High German Heimrich, built from words for home and ruler. It has been recorded in Sweden since 1208.
namesakes: Henrik Ibsen (Norwegian playwright of A Doll's House)
Henrik Lundqvist (New York Rangers goaltender)

e.etymology: The English word for faithful allegiance, from Old French loialte, ultimately from Latin legalis (of the law). It is a recent American virtue name, given mostly to girls.
A spelling variant of Xavier that writes the name the way Americans say it. Xavier comes from the Basque place name Etxeberria (new house), birthplace of Saint Francis Xavier.

From an English surname that preserves the Old English name Deorwine, from deore (dear) and wine (friend). Naturalist Charles Darwin made the surname famous, and it is now a popular first name in Latin America.
namesakes: Darwin Watterson (goldfish in The Amazing World of Gumball)

assoc.t: naturalist Charles Darwin and the theory of evolution
the Darwin Awards for fatally foolish acts

e.note: Most people hear Charles Darwin and evolution first; expect the occasional Darwin Awards joke.

e.etymology: A modern name used mostly in Puerto Rican and other Caribbean Hispanic families. It follows the pattern of biblical names ending in -iel, such as Adiel and Uriel; no documented meaning is attached.
A modern American coinage that fits Kai- or Kay- onto the -sley ending of Paisley, Kinsley and Ainsley.
From the Spanish noun esperanza (hope), from Latin sperare (to hope). It is one of the traditional Spanish virtue names, also used as a title of the Virgin Mary.
namesakes: Esperanza Spalding (Grammy-winning jazz bassist and singer)
Esperanza Cordero (narrator of The House on Mango Street)
Esperanza Ortega (heroine of the novel Esperanza Rising)

assoc.t: Esperanza, heroine of the novel Esperanza Rising

e.etymology: In Arabic, Dania (also Daniya) means near or close at hand. The name is also used in Spanish-speaking families, where it is felt as a relative of Daniela, and Dania is the Latin name of Denmark.
A phonetic respelling of Malia, the Hawaiian form of Maria (Mary). It peaked in 2009, the year Malia Obama moved into the White House.

A variant of Colby, an English place name and surname from Old Norse: either the personal name Koli or kol (charcoal) plus byr (settlement). Singer Colbie Caillat made this spelling familiar for girls.
namesakes: Colbie Caillat (singer of Bubbly)

e.meaning: thought to mean devotee of Marduk
e.etymology: The Hebrew form of Mordecai, the cousin and guardian of Esther who helps save the Jews in the Book of Esther. Scholars link the name to Marduk, the chief god of Babylon, where the story's exiles lived.
namesakes: Mordecai (Esther's cousin and guardian in the Book of Esther)

e.etymology: Two unrelated names. The Japanese girls' name is usually understood as lily, though it can be written with other characters. The Russian boys' name is a form of George, from Greek georgos (farmer).
namesakes: Yuri Gagarin (Soviet cosmonaut, first human in space)
Yuri Zhivago (hero of Doctor Zhivago)

assoc.t: yuri, anime and manga genre of romance between women
Yuri on Ice, figure skating anime

e.note: Among anime and manga fans, yuri is the name of the genre about romance between women.

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Camden, an English place name and surname usually explained as Old English for enclosed valley.
The Italian feminine of Paolo, from the Latin family name Paulus (small, humble). It is the Italian counterpart of Paula and is widely used in Latin America.
A modern American invention that joins the Jaz- of Jasmine to the -lynn ending.
A respelling of Leilani, a Hawaiian name made from lei (garland of flowers) and lani (heaven, sky; royal).

e.meaning: pet form of Randall or Randolph, shield wolf
e.etymology: A pet form of Randall and Randolph, which come from Germanic words for shield rim and wolf; occasionally also short for Miranda. Americans made it a given name in its own right in the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Randy Jackson (American Idol judge)
Randy Travis (country singer)
Randy Johnson (Hall of Fame pitcher)
e.note: In British and Commonwealth English, randy is everyday slang for sexually aroused.

e.etymology: A modern American name of unclear origin, that became common around 2000 alongside Aniyah, Aaliyah and Amiya. It may be an elaboration of Anya, the Russian pet form of Anna; some name books call it Hebrew.
The English word, unchanged since Old English, used as a given name for girls and boys. Storm is also an old surname and a given name in Scandinavia and the Netherlands.
namesakes: Storm Reid (actress in Euphoria and A Wrinkle in Time)
Storm (weather-controlling X-Men hero)

e.etymology: A modern name with no settled origin. It echoes Eleni, the Greek form of Helen, and Hawaiian names ending in -lani (heaven) such as Leilani and Kailani.
The German, Scandinavian and Slavic form of Stephen, from Greek stephanos (wreath, crown). Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr, spread the name across Europe.
namesakes: Stefan Salvatore (vampire brother in The Vampire Diaries)
Stefan Edberg (Swedish tennis champion)
Stefan Urquelle (Steve Urkel's suave alter ego on Family Matters)

e.etymology: A modern American name with no settled source. It shares its sound with Breckenridge, the Colorado ski town, and with the Irish surname Bracken, from breac (speckled).
A recent name with no documented origin. It resembles Israel, Ismael and Azael, and is found mostly in Hispanic families.
A modern respelling of Corbin, an English and French surname from Old French corbin (raven, crow), first a nickname for someone with dark hair.
A Spanish-language respelling of Giovanni, the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan (God is gracious). The J spelling is used mostly in Hispanic families.

A Spanish-language name used mostly in Puerto Rican and other Caribbean families, and the stage name of a Puerto Rican reggaeton singer. It resembles the biblical Hebrew name Jahdiel, which ends in El (God).
The English word for sovereign grandeur and a form of address for kings and queens, from Latin maiestas (greatness). It is a recent American word name, given to girls more than boys.

e.meaning: pet form of Alexandra or Alexis, defender of men
e.etymology: A clipped pet form of Alexis, Alexia, Alexandra and Alexandria, all from the Greek verb alexein (to defend). It has been given as a full name since the 1990s.
namesakes: Lexie Grey (surgeon on Grey's Anatomy)

e.etymology: From a northern English and Scottish surname taken from places named in Old Norse with kross (cross) and byr (settlement).

assoc.t: Bing Crosby, crooner of White Christmas
Crosby, Stills & Nash, folk rock band
